opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and I should say upfront that I can only speak from my own experience and what I've seen from the outside. Every lab changes its structure pretty often, so take this as a personal impression, not an org chart.

The traditional way to divide things is by training stage: a pretraining team, a post-training team, maybe an RL or reasoning team, plus infrastructure, data, and evaluation. In that model, pretraining builds the base model, and post-training turns it into something useful. Almost every lab started roughly like this, because it mirrors how the pipeline actually runs.

What I find interesting about OpenAI is that, at least as it appears from the outside, the boundaries have become more fluid and more organized around capabilities or bets than around pipeline stages. A reasoning effort, for example, isn't really "post-training" in the old sense. It cuts across data, RL infrastructure, evaluation, and even what you want from the base model. So you see small teams that own a capability end to end and can move very fast. That fits a culture where a few people with strong conviction can push a direction hard before it's obvious to everyone else.

Other labs make different trade-offs. Some keep a more unified, centralized research agenda, where one main model line gets everyone's effort and you coordinate tightly around it. That gives you consistency and less duplicated work, but it can be slower to explore something unusual. Others are very research-driven, with many parallel directions, and the challenge becomes integrating them into one product model.

In the end I don't think one structure is simply better. The deeper question is how a lab handles the interface between "making the model smarter" and "making the model useful." As RL and reasoning matter more, that interface becomes the most important place in the organization. Whoever designs that boundary well, so that pretraining people understand what downstream needs and post-training people can feed back into the base model, will have a real advantage. Org structure is really a bet on where the next breakthrough will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so this is actually a question I get asked a lot, and I think the first thing to say is that from the outside the division looks cleaner than it actually is from the inside.

The classic way people describe OpenAI is: there's a pre-training team, and there's a post-training team. Pre-training is the people who build the base model, who worry about data, scaling laws, architecture, the infrastructure for very large runs. Post-training is everything after that: SFT, RLHF, and now increasingly RL with verifiable rewards, reasoning, agents. And then there's a reasoning effort, which I'd say is really where the center of gravity has moved in the last couple of years. When o1 came out, that was essentially the reasoning group's work, and that reshaped how the whole company thinks about what the training stack even is.

Compared with other labs, I'd point to a few differences.

One is that OpenAI, historically, has been more willing to make a bet and reorganize around it. Reasoning was a bet. Agents are a bet. When the bet starts paying off, the org chart follows the result rather than the other way around. Some other labs are organized more around persistent functions, like you have a "model behavior" team or an "alignment" team that stays stable, and projects flow through them. Neither is strictly better. OpenAI's approach gets you speed and a clear owner for a direction, but you pay a cost in churn.

Another difference is the boundary between research and product. At OpenAI the product side is very close to the training teams. The people doing post-training are often looking at real usage, real failure cases, and feeding that back in. In a more academic setting, like where I came from, you don't have that loop at all. You build a benchmark, you optimize for it, and then you wonder why nobody uses the thing. At a lab, the user is the benchmark, in a sense. That changes what "training" means.

The third thing I'd say, and this is my personal view, is that the line between pre-training and post-training is getting blurrier, and I think that's true everywhere, not just at OpenAI. When you do large-scale RL on reasoning, the compute is starting to look like pre-training compute. The data pipelines start to look similar. So the teams that were separate for historical reasons start to overlap, and you see people moving back and forth. I think in a few years the question "which team are you on" will have a less interesting answer than it does today, because the real unit will be: what environment are you training in, what reward are you optimizing, and what capability are you trying to unlock.

From my own angle, coming from working on agents, what I care about is whoever owns the environments. That's the piece that I think is still under-built across all the labs. You can have beautiful pre-training and beautiful RL algorithms, but if the environments the model learns in are narrow, the model is narrow. So if you ask me how I understand the division, I'd say the honest answer is that the most important team is the one whose name hasn't quite stabilized yet.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it in terms of the stages of training, rather than just the team names. Broadly, pretraining builds the model’s underlying capabilities, while post-training shapes how those capabilities show up in use: whether the model follows instructions, reasons effectively, uses tools, and gives helpful answers.

But I wouldn’t claim to know the exact internal division at OpenAI or every other lab. Similar team names can cover quite different responsibilities. For example, reinforcement learning might sit within post-training, or it might become a substantial research effort of its own.

To me, the more interesting question is how closely those teams work together. Something that looks like a post-training limitation may actually require better pretraining data, and a capability learned during pretraining may only become useful with the right post-training setup. So the organizational boundaries matter, but the feedback across those boundaries matters just as much.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinforcement learning as a possible part of post-training, but does not identify OpenAI’s Strawberry group or compare it with other companies’ terminology.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify OpenAI’s post-training group as corresponding to what other AI companies call product.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that OpenAI’s division is relatively centered on stages of training: pretraining builds the foundation, and post-training turns that foundation into a useful assistant. As reasoning becomes more important, reinforcement learning also becomes a major part of the work, with its own demands around data, environments, and evaluation.

But I’d be careful about drawing a precise organizational chart from the outside. Other labs use similar terms, and the actual boundaries can be quite different. The more interesting question is how closely these teams work together. A limitation you see in an agent might come from the base model, from post-training, or from the environment and tools. You need feedback to travel across those boundaries rather than treating each stage as an isolated problem.
